title: Built-in agents
standfirst: Some providers ship the machine with coding agents already installed and a way to prompt them. Others ship a computer and expect you to bring the agent.
idea: A preinstalled agent is not a hosted agent. Preinstalled means the binary is on the disk and a login may be configured; the agent loop still runs inside your sandbox and you still pay the model provider, or sign in with your own subscription. Hosted means the provider runs the loop and bills you for it.

The useful distinction is threefold: is an agent installed, can you prompt it through the provider's API rather than a terminal, and does the provider manage the model credentials? Very few do all three.

Preinstalled agents also change the setup story. A machine with Claude Code and Codex already on it is a working environment for a non-engineer who can type a request, even if nothing else is click-driven.

splits.heading: Installed and promptable
body: Boat installs seven harnesses and exposes a prompt endpoint with steering, interrupts and multiple conversations. Sandboxer installs six and has a prompt API with an event stream. Agent 37 has six agent templates plus a separate managed-hosting product where the agent is the product.
Lizard installs five and prompts them from the CLI only; the SDK has no prompt method. boxd installs three and relies on the in-VM CLI.

splits.heading: Installed, not managed
body: InstaBox and Vercel put coding agents in their default images but publish no agent-run API: you open a terminal and use them. E2B documents how to run Claude Code, Codex and Amp, but does not claim to preinstall them.
That is enough for a technical user and not enough for a product that wants to start an agent on demand.

splits.heading: Bring your own
body: Runtime does not preinstall agents, and its own docs say no bridge harness has run on it yet. Sprites offers plugins and SDK integrations rather than a hosted agent. Morph exposes a tmux API so an agent can be driven programmatically, but the agent is yours.
At these providers the sandbox is the product and the agent is an application you install.

watchFor: Whether the agent is preinstalled, promptable through an API, or both.
Who pays for the model: the provider, your API key, or your subscription login.
Whether the provider manages model credentials or expects them in the environment.
Whether the agent runs as a hosted service or inside your sandbox.
Whether a non-engineer can start it without a terminal.

scenario.title: Send a task and read the stream back
scenario.setup: You want to post a prompt to a sandbox and receive the agent's output as a stream, without opening a terminal or holding a model key inside the machine.

beats.what: The agent binary is either on the disk already or something your setup script installs.
One API call with a prompt, or a shell command typed by a person.
The model bill goes to the provider, to your API key, or to your subscription login.

scenario.turn: Only a few providers do all three: installed, promptable through their API, and managing the model credentials. Everywhere else the sandbox is the product and the agent is an application you bring.

questions: Is the agent preinstalled, promptable through your API, or both?
Who pays for the model — you, my API key, or my subscription login?
Does the provider manage model credentials, or expect them in the environment?
Does the agent loop run inside my sandbox or as a hosted service, and what does that change about billing?
Can a non-engineer start it without a terminal, and what is the first screen they see?
